summary.text:
Cheshire Fire Authority's 2025-26 outturn is a small book — £11,119k of PWLB borrowing at 31 March 2026, sitting against £14,001k of treasury investments — but the paper reconciles unusually cleanly. Para 14 (p3) names the three Training Centre loans by draw date and rate: £4m at 1.99% (March 2021), £4m at 1.65% (July 2021), £3m at 1.63% (November 2021). Our file holds exactly those three loans at exactly those rates, plus a fourth £119k loan at 5.38% maturing 2027-03-31 that appears in Table 3's 12-24 month bucket (£119k, 1% of the book) but is not narrated. Four loans, £11,119,000, weighted 1.8068% — matches to the £1 and to under half a basis point on the long-loan average.

The balance sheet closes on the classical identity: CFR £23,853k − External borrowing £11,119k − OLTL £0 = £12,734k internal borrowing, 53.4% of CFR. The paper carries its own 'Internal/Over borrowing' line at £8,166k against a 'Gross borrowing requirement' of £18,119k, using a base £5,734k below CFR — we do not hold the reconciliation between those two definitions, and the paper does not print it, so any cross-council comparison uses the classical £12,734k.

The forward story is the Liability Benchmark peak at para 33 (p7): rising to ~£21m in 2028 against an existing portfolio flat at ~£11m — the ~£10m 'white triangle' the paper describes at para 34 as needing borrowing for durations up to around 20 years. Para 27 identifies the projects (Wilmslow day-crewing houses, Crewe Fire Station rebuild — £11.5m total), and para 39 says the Authority does not expect to need external borrowing until later in 2026-27. Table 1 (p2) shows their current view of PWLB rates as 4.99%–6.46% across 1-50 years, and para 25 records that the ~1% new-borrowing/repayment differential 'made rescheduling unviable'. Our break-cost engine agrees on the underlying arithmetic — the three long 1.6-2.0% loans stand at a net indicative discount of £6.7m (60% of principal) against today's 6%+ long curve, but whether anything is worth doing turns on replacement cost, MRP and accounting treatment we do not model, so the paper's 'unviable' conclusion is not something we contest.

Two small paper artefacts to note internally only: the Treasury Indicators sub-table on p8 is headed '2024/25' but the numbers are unambiguously 2025-26 (Actual external debt £11,119k), and '23.317' for the authorised-limit outturn uses a period rather than a comma. Both are typesetting slips and are the kind of thing the template's 'never invite them to correct us' rule was written for. No officer email address is printed anywhere in the paper — the contact block on p9 names Kirsty Jennings, Governance Manager, with a phone number only. The report author is James Cunningham, Head of Finance and Treasurer, who is the Fire Authority's s151-equivalent.

officer.body:
Hi James,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority and combined-authority treasury teams: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, your own PWLB book laid against ours, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every authority in the country, so we can see how a body's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. Below are a couple of thoughts on your 2025-26 Treasury Management Annual Report, which went to the Authority on 24 June. You're not being singled out — every authority we hold papers for gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it. Your report is unusually specific about the loans it names, which is what lets a reader outside the authority reconcile the whole book without any inference.

The tie first, because it settles whether we've actually read the paper. Your paragraph 14 names three PWLB loans by draw date and rate: £4m at 1.99% (March 2021), £4m at 1.65% (July 2021), £3m at 1.63% (November 2021). We hold exactly those three loans at exactly those rates, on ~50-year maturities running from 2069 to 2071. Your Table 3 also shows £119k of debt in the 12-24 month bucket that the narrative doesn't cover — that reconciles to a fourth PWLB maturing on 31 March 2027 at 5.38%. Four loans, £11,119,000 in total, at a weighted 1.8068%. The three long loans on their own weight to 1.7682% — our over-25-year bucket for you sits at 1.768%, so under half a basis point either way. That is your Table 2 and your Table 3 tying to our file to the £1, without either side having to translate anything.

On the balance sheet the classical identity closes. Your CFR of £23,853k less external borrowing of £11,119k less zero other long-term liabilities is £12,734k of internal borrowing — 53% of the CFR carried from your own cash. That is what your paragraph 39 is describing when it says the Authority does not expect to need external borrowing until later in 2026-27, and what your recommendation [3] is asking members to keep supporting. It's a large internal position relative to the total book, and the shape of the paper puts a clock on it: paragraph 33 has the Liability Benchmark peaking in around 2028, paragraph 34 has the 'white triangular period between 2026 and 2038' that ideally gets filled with borrowing 'for a range of durations up to around 20 years', and paragraph 27 names the projects — Wilmslow day-crewing houses and Crewe Fire Station rebuild at £11.5m in total — so the 2028 peak has a driver and a date attached to it.

We host a liability benchmark tool at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity that lets you replay that same shape against the daily PWLB curve — useful mostly for the timing question, given your paragraph 39's own view is that later in 2026-27 is when the decision arrives.

One thing not to over-read. Your paragraph 25 records that the ~1% differential between PWLB new-borrowing rates and premature repayment rates 'made rescheduling unviable' this year. On our indicative pricing your three long loans stand at a large nominal discount to par against today's long curve — but that's a function of holding 1.6-2.0% money against 6%+ replacement, and whether the arithmetic actually pays turns on replacement cost, MRP treatment and accounting we don't model. The DMO's quote is the only binding one. Our engine agrees the position is unviable on those terms — it's not a critique.

On training, two short courses fit what's above: PWLB explained, for anyone newer to the certainty-rate mechanics behind the 2027-28 borrowing decision, and Liability benchmarks in practice, given yours sits at the centre of the paper. All 115 courses are free to local authorities and combined authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, with free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find any of this useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
